title: The Royal Navy retires the cutlass, 1936 — and the boarding that came after
sources: Wikipedia: Cutlass — a short, broad sabre, a common naval weapon in the Age of Sail; robust enough to cut through heavy ropes and canvas, short enough for close combat in boarding actions, in the rigging or below decks; simple to use; famous as a pirate weapon (William Kidd, Stede Bonnet); in 1936 the Royal Navy announced cutlasses would be carried only for ceremonial duties and not used in landing parties; the last recorded use is often said to be 16 February 1940 in the Altmark incident, but this is disputed — the HMS Cossack Association and the authors of British Naval Swords and Swordsmanship disbelieve it, and think the last use was by a shore party in China in 1900; cutlasses are still worn by Chief Petty Officers escorting the White Ensign

Wikipedia: Altmark incident — in February 1940 the German tanker Altmark carried 299 captured British sailors; HMS Cossack, under Philip Vian, followed her into Jøssingfjord, boarded her and liberated the prisoners
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1907 a bank run forces the Knickerbocker Trust Company to suspend operations; 2008 India launches Chandrayaan-1, its first lunar probe

Pictures (public domain): boys at cutlass drill aboard HMS Wolverine, 1882; British sailors boarding an Algerine pirate ship; François l'Olonnais (1678); HMS Cossack; the Altmark in Jøssingfjord; RAF photo of the Altmark; HMS Cossack returns to Leith, 17 February 1940
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): rough sea, a sailing ship's masts

post.facebook:
In 1936, the Royal Navy announced that its sailors' cutlasses would be carried only for ceremonial duties — never again in landing parties.

The cutlass was a short, broad sabre: short enough for close fighting below decks or in the rigging, strong enough to hack through heavy rope and canvas, and simple to use. Boys in the navy drilled with it, and pirates were famous for it. It was the weapon of the boarding party.

But the story has a famous postscript. In February 1940 the German ship Altmark hid in a Norwegian fjord with 299 captured British sailors aboard. The destroyer HMS Cossack went in, boarded her, and set them free — and legend says it was the last time the Royal Navy boarded with cutlasses. Many historians doubt it: they think the last real use was by a shore party in China in 1900.

Today, chief petty officers still carry a cutlass when they escort the White Ensign.

Also on 22 October: a run on the Knickerbocker Trust set off the Panic of 1907, and India launched Chandrayaan-1, its first Moon probe (2008).

youtube.description:
In 1936 the Royal Navy retired the cutlass from fighting — from then on, it was for ceremony only. Short, broad and simple, it was the sailor's sword for three centuries: the weapon of boarding parties and pirates. Legend says it was used one last time in February 1940, when HMS Cossack boarded the German ship Altmark in a Norwegian fjord and freed 299 British prisoners — but many historians believe the real last use was by a shore party in China in 1900.

Also on 22 October: the Knickerbocker Trust bank run (1907) and India's Chandrayaan-1 (2008).
